title: What is Delta Lake's `MERGE INTO` (upsert) — atomically match rows and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in one statement — and how does it compare to a manual read-check-write pattern (MERGE is atomic and handles concurrency)?

s1_definition.profdef: `MERGE INTO` is Delta Lake's atomic upsert operation. It joins a target table with a source dataset on a matching condition and, in a single transaction, applies `WHEN MATCHED` actions (UPDATE or DELETE) and `WHEN NOT MATCHED` actions (INSERT). Because it commits as one Delta transaction, it is atomic and isolated, unlike a hand-written read-check-then-write sequence that can race with concurrent writers and leave the table inconsistent.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank gets a nightly file of balance changes. For each account, if it already exists, update the balance; if it is new, insert it; if it is closed, delete it. Doing this by hand means reading each account, checking, then writing — and if two clerks do this at once, they can overwrite each other. `MERGE INTO` is one clerk who does the whole match-and-apply in a single locked step, so the result is always correct.
s1_definition.oneliner: MERGE INTO is a single atomic upsert that matches source to target and applies UPDATE, DELETE, and INSERT together, safely under concurrency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `MERGE INTO` is Delta Lake's atomic upsert operation. It joins a target table with a source dataset on a matching condition and, in a single transaction, applies `WHEN MATCHED` actions (UPDATE or DELETE) and `WHEN NOT MATCHED` actions (INSERT). Because it commits as one Delta transaction, it is atomic and isolated, unlike a hand-written read-check-then-write sequence that can race with concurrent writers and leave the table inconsistent.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank gets a nightly file of balance changes. For each account, if it already exists, update the balance; if it is new, insert it; if it is closed, delete it. Doing this by hand means reading each account, checking, then writing — and if two clerks do this at once, they can overwrite each other. `MERGE INTO` is one clerk who does the whole match-and-apply in a single locked step, so the result is always correct.

**One line to remember:** MERGE INTO is a single atomic upsert that matches source to target and applies UPDATE, DELETE, and INSERT together, safely under concurrency.

sections.s2_technical:
A MERGE has three parts: the target Delta table, the source DataFrame or table, and an ON condition that defines a match (usually a business key). Then you specify branches. `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ...` updates existing rows, `WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE` removes them, and `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ...` adds new rows. You can add conditions to branches, for example `WHEN MATCHED AND source.status = 'CLOSED' THEN DELETE`.

In the DataFrame API it reads naturally: `DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).alias("t").merge(source.alias("s"), "t.account_id = s.account_id").whenMatchedUpdate(set={"balance": "s.balance"}).whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute()`.

The contrast with a manual pattern is the key interview point. A manual upsert reads the target, computes which rows to update or insert in the driver or another job, and writes them back. Between the read and the write, another writer can change the table, so your write is based on stale state and you lose updates or create duplicates. MERGE avoids this because Delta performs the join and the writes inside one optimistic transaction, detecting conflicting commits and failing or retrying rather than silently corrupting data. It is also far more efficient, rewriting only the files that contain matched rows rather than the whole table.

A senior nuance: MERGE can be expensive if the match condition touches many files, so you narrow it with partition or ZORDER predicates and avoid multiple matches per target row, which Delta rejects to keep results deterministic. You also use `whenNotMatchedBySourceDelete` to remove target rows absent from the source when doing full-sync upserts.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank receives a nightly change file: some accounts have new balances, some are brand new, and some are closed. Applying this with a read-check-write loop risks losing concurrent updates. This is exactly what MERGE's atomic upsert solves.

Problem 2 — New accounts must be inserted, existing ones updated, and closed ones deleted, all in one pass. This maps directly to the three MERGE branches.

Problem 3 — The operation must be safe even if another job writes to the same table at the same time. This is the concurrency and atomicity guarantee MERGE provides over a manual pattern.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`MergeUpsertDemo`) that starts with a balances table for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), then applies a change file that updates Rajesh, inserts a new account, and closes Priya — all in one MERGE.

##### 4b. SQL / Delta DDL Script

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS balances_merge (
    account_id STRING, balance DECIMAL(15,2), status STRING
) USING DELTA LOCATION '/data/warehouse/balances_merge';

-- Equivalent SQL MERGE
MERGE INTO balances_merge t
USING changes s
ON t.account_id = s.account_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.status = 'CLOSED' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.balance = s.balance, t.status = s.status
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (account_id, balance, status)
                      VALUES (s.account_id, s.balance, s.status);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```text
# spark-defaults.conf
spark.sql.extensions            io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension
spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog
```
sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/merge_upsert_demo.py
# Atomic upsert of a nightly change file for the National Bank of India.
import logging
from decimal import Decimal
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from upsert.balance_merger import BalanceMerger

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("MergeUpsertDemo")
PATH = "/data/warehouse/balances_merge"

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("MergeUpsertDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
            .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                    "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
            .getOrCreate())

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    # Initial target: Rajesh and Priya both ACTIVE
    target = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", Decimal("1000000.00"), "ACTIVE"),
         ("CUR3001", Decimal("250000.00"),  "ACTIVE")],
        ["account_id", "balance", "status"])
    target.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(PATH)
    log.info("Initial balances written")

    # Nightly change file: UPDATE Rajesh, INSERT new SAV2002, CLOSE (delete) Priya
    changes = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("SAV2001", Decimal("1050000.00"), "ACTIVE"),   # update
         ("SAV2002", Decimal("75000.00"),   "ACTIVE"),   # insert
         ("CUR3001", Decimal("0.00"),       "CLOSED")],  # delete
        ["account_id", "balance", "status"])

    BalanceMerger(spark, PATH).apply(changes)            # one atomic MERGE
    log.info("After MERGE (upsert):")
    spark.read.format("delta").load(PATH).orderBy("account_id").show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/upsert/balance_merger.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, DataFrame
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

class BalanceMerger:
    """Encapsulates an atomic upsert of balance changes into a Delta table."""
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession, path: str):
        self.spark = spark
        self.path = path

    def apply(self, changes: DataFrame) -> None:
        target = DeltaTable.forPath(self.spark, self.path)
        (target.alias("t")
            .merge(changes.alias("s"), "t.account_id = s.account_id")
            # closed accounts are deleted
            .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.status = 'CLOSED'")
            # existing accounts are updated
            .whenMatchedUpdate(set={"balance": "s.balance", "status": "s.status"})
            # new accounts are inserted
            .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
            .execute())
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: target has SAV2001 and CUR3001 both ACTIVE; change file updates SAV2001, inserts SAV2002, closes CUR3001.

Step 1: The initial write creates the target table with two ACTIVE accounts.

Step 2: MERGE joins target and source on `account_id`. SAV2001 matches, CUR3001 matches, SAV2002 does not.

Step 3: The CLOSED branch fires first for CUR3001 because its source status is CLOSED, so CUR3001 is deleted.

Step 4: The UPDATE branch fires for SAV2001, setting its balance to 1,050,000.

Step 5: The INSERT branch fires for SAV2002, adding it with 75,000.

Step 6: All three changes commit as one Delta transaction, so a concurrent reader sees either the whole before state or the whole after state, never a partial mix.


sections.s6_takeaway:
MERGE INTO is Delta Lake's atomic upsert. I give it a target table, a source dataset, and an ON condition that defines what counts as a match, usually a business key. Then I specify branches: WHEN MATCHED can UPDATE or DELETE, and WHEN NOT MATCHED can INSERT, and I can guard each branch with a condition such as deleting only rows whose source status is CLOSED. The whole thing commits as one Delta transaction, so it is atomic and isolated, and it rewrites only the files that actually contain matched rows rather than the whole table.

The reason this matters is the contrast with a hand-written read-check-write pattern. In the manual approach I read the target, figure out which rows to update or insert, and write them back, but between my read and my write another job can change the table, so my write is based on stale state and I either lose updates or create duplicates. MERGE avoids that entirely because Delta performs the join and the writes inside a single optimistic transaction and detects conflicting commits, so it either succeeds cleanly or retries instead of silently corrupting data.

At the National Bank of India we used MERGE for the nightly balance change file. Each night some accounts had new balances, some were brand new, and some were closed, and I applied all three cases in one statement: a matched-and-closed branch that deleted, a matched branch that updated the balance, and a not-matched branch that inserted new accounts. Because it was a single atomic commit, a report running at the same time always saw a consistent snapshot, never a half-applied file. The caution I mention is to keep the match condition narrow using partition or ZORDER predicates so MERGE touches few files, and to make sure the source never matches a target row more than once, since Delta rejects that to keep the result deterministic.
